topics.title: Quality Foundations: IOM Aims, National Initiatives & Related Concepts
topics.summary: Quality is not a feeling or a slogan; it is care that makes good outcomes more likely and matches current evidence. This lesson builds the vocabulary (quality, QI, quality management, the IOM Six Aims) and the national landscape (NDNQI, NPSGs, ACA, AHRQ priorities) that every later QI decision rests on.
objectives: Define quality, quality improvement (QI), and quality management and explain how each shows up in a staff nurse’s shift.
Explain why the IOM reports To Err Is Human and Crossing the Quality Chasm shifted the focus from blaming individuals to redesigning systems.
Apply the IOM Six Aims (safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, equitable) to classify real bedside actions and choose the aim an action best supports.
Describe the three major nursing quality efforts (NDNQI, the AHRQ evidence-based handbook, and The Joint Commission National Patient Safety Goals) and use them to answer bedside questions.
Connect the Affordable Care Act, readmission penalties, bundled payments, and the AHRQ National Quality Strategy to specific nursing actions such as discharge teaching and care coordination.
Relate ethics, informatics, and legal issues to quality and choose the nursing action that protects clients’ rights, records, and safety.
Use a repeatable strategy to answer NCLEX items that ask which action best reflects a quality aim or safety goal.
topics.bigPicture:
Every hospital you will ever work in is constantly measuring itself: How many clients fell? How many developed a pressure injury or a catheter infection? How many came back within 30 days? Those numbers are not paperwork for managers. They are the trail your own nursing care leaves behind. When you reassess pain within an hour, use two identifiers, or teach a heart failure client to weigh daily, you are producing the data that tell the organization whether its care is actually quality care.

The modern quality movement began with an uncomfortable finding: large numbers of clients are harmed by the care meant to help them, and most of that harm comes from flawed systems, not bad people. The Institute of Medicine (IOM) reports reframed safety as a design problem and gave health care a shared target, the Six Aims. Federal programs, accrediting bodies, and payers now reward organizations that hit those targets and penalize those that do not, which is why nurses are asked to participate in QI committees, audits, and new protocols.

On the NCLEX this content rarely appears as “define quality.” Instead you will see a nurse, a client, and a choice: Which action best reflects patient-centered care? Which response to a new nurse shows a systems view of error? Which initiative would most directly reduce readmissions? This lesson teaches you to translate each abstract aim or initiative into the concrete nursing behavior the item is looking for.

keyTerms.def: The degree to which health services for individuals and populations increase the likelihood of desired health outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge. Includes technically competent care, good communication, shared decision-making, and cultural sensitivity.
Systematic and continuous actions that lead to measurable improvement in health care services and in the health status of targeted client groups.

Evaluation of medical and nursing processes for quality and effectiveness compared with accepted standards, so that problems are corrected before they harm clients and errors in treatment are prevented; also aims for cost-effective care by preventing overuse, misuse, and underuse of resources.

keyTerms.term: To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System
keyTerms.def: Landmark IOM report (released 1999, published 2000) estimating up to 98,000 U.S. deaths per year from medical errors and concluding that most errors arise from faulty systems rather than careless individuals.
IOM report finding the health care system too disorganized to meet the needs of people with multiple chronic illnesses; established the Six Aims for improvement.

keyTerms.term: Six Aims for Improving the Health Care System
keyTerms.def: Care should be Safe, Effective, Patient-centered, Timely, Efficient, and Equitable (often remembered as STEEEP).
Avoiding injuries to clients from the care that is intended to help them.
Providing services based on scientific knowledge to all who could benefit and refraining from providing services to those not likely to benefit (avoiding underuse and overuse).
Providing care that is respectful of and responsive to individual client preferences, needs, and values, ensuring client values guide all clinical decisions.
Reducing waits and sometimes harmful delays for both those who receive and those who give care.
Avoiding waste, including waste of equipment, supplies, ideas, and energy.
Providing care that does not vary in quality because of personal characteristics such as gender, ethnicity, geographic location, or socioeconomic status.
Systematic reviews report an overall median medication error rate of roughly 19.6%–25.6% of administrations studied, showing how common medication errors are.

keyTerms.term: National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators (NDNQI)
keyTerms.def: National database of nursing-sensitive indicators (such as falls, pressure injuries, CAUTI, skill mix) that lets units compare their performance with similar units.

keyTerms.term: Patient Safety and Quality: An Evidence-Based Handbook for Nurses
keyTerms.def: AHRQ publication summarizing the evidence on nursing’s role in safety and quality; one of the three major nursing quality efforts.

Annual, specific safety requirements published by The Joint Commission (for example, use two client identifiers, improve communication of critical results, use medicines safely, prevent infection, identify suicide risk, prevent surgical mistakes).

keyTerms.term: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA, 2010)
keyTerms.def: Federal law that expanded and reformed Medicaid and Medicare, created incentives (including penalties) to reduce 30-day readmissions, and created incentives to reduce wasteful spending.

National framework with three broad aims (Better Care, Healthy People/Healthy Communities, Affordable Care) pursued through six priorities: patient safety, person- and family-centered care, care coordination, effective prevention and treatment (starting with cardiovascular disease), healthy living, and affordability.
Optional state program under the ACA, federally subsidized, that provides coverage for low-income adults and lawfully present immigrants who are not eligible for Medicaid.

A single payment for all services in an episode of care (for example, a joint replacement from surgery through recovery); rewards coordination and has reduced costs, especially for orthopedic procedures.
Standardized, evidence-based clinical benchmarks tracked for specific conditions (for example, stroke and myocardial infarction discharge medications and follow-up).
Measured rates such as infection rates, fall rates, and pressure injury incidence that quality programs track over time.
Survey used by facilities to assess whether staff feel comfortable reporting errors and how they perceive teamwork and safety.
Use of electronic records and data at the point of care to improve continuity, track health care-associated infections (HAIs), and identify areas lacking resources.

Legal documents expressing a person’s health care wishes (living will, health care proxy/power of attorney) and related orders such as DNR; nurses ask about them as part of legally sound, quality care.

sections.heading: What quality means and why the IOM reports changed everything
sections.body:
The IOM (now the National Academy of Medicine) defines quality as the degree to which health services increase the likelihood of desired outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge. Notice two things. First, quality is about probability: you cannot guarantee a good outcome, but you can make it more likely. Second, quality is tied to current evidence: yesterday’s routine can become today’s poor quality. Quality also includes more than technical skill: good communication, shared decision-making, and cultural sensitivity are part of the definition. A nurse who starts a perfect IV but never asks the client what matters to them has delivered only part of quality care.

Quality improvement (QI) (HRSA definition) is the systematic and continuous work that produces measurable improvement in services and in the health status of targeted groups. Quality management is the broader evaluation of medical and nursing processes against accepted standards, aimed at correcting problems before they harm clients and at preventing overuse, misuse, and underuse of resources.

To Err Is Human reported that up to 98,000 people die each year in U.S. hospitals from medical errors; a later Johns Hopkins analysis estimated more than 250,000 deaths per year, which would make medical error a leading cause of death. Systematic reviews show a median medication error rate of about 19.6%–25.6%. The report’s most important message was not the number; it was the cause: most errors come from faulty systems, processes, and conditions that lead good people to make mistakes. Crossing the Quality Chasm (2001) then described a system too disorganized for people with multiple chronic conditions and set the Six Aims.
sections.analogy: Think of an airline. When a plane nearly crashes, investigators do not just fire the pilot; they ask why the checklist, the cockpit design, and the communication allowed the mistake. The IOM asked health care to think the same way: design the cockpit so that a tired, interrupted, competent nurse still cannot easily give the wrong drug.

check.q: A new graduate says, “If everyone were just more careful, we wouldn’t have medication errors.” Which IOM conclusion contradicts this statement?
check.a: To Err Is Human found that most errors result from faulty systems and processes, not individual carelessness, so the fix is redesigning systems (barcode scanning, standardized processes) and encouraging reporting.

sections.heading: The Six Aims (STEEEP): turning words into nursing actions
sections.body:
The Six Aims are the most testable part of this section because each aim can be matched to a concrete behavior. The NCLEX will describe an action and ask which aim it represents, or describe an aim and ask which action fulfills it. The trick is to focus on the problem the action prevents: injury (safe), care that does not match evidence (effective), care that ignores the person (patient-centered), harmful delay (timely), waste (efficient), or unequal quality between groups (equitable).

Two pairs cause most errors. Effective vs. efficient: effective is about evidence and benefit (giving what helps, withholding what does not; avoiding underuse and overuse); efficient is about waste of resources (supplies, equipment, time, ideas, energy). Patient-centered vs. equitable: patient-centered asks “What does this person value?”; equitable asks “Does the quality differ across groups?” Using a qualified interpreter so a Spanish-speaking client receives the same pain reassessment as English-speaking clients is primarily about equitable quality; letting a client choose the timing of a bath to match their routine is patient-centered.

rows: Safe
Could the care itself hurt the client?
Two identifiers before blood; bed alarm for a high fall-risk client
injury, harm, error, prevent
Effective
Is the care supported by evidence and given to those who benefit?
Evidence-based VTE prophylaxis for eligible clients; not giving antibiotics for a viral cold
evidence, benefit, overuse, underuse
Patient-centered
Do the client’s values and preferences guide decisions?
Planning care around a client’s prayer times; shared goal-setting for pain
preferences, values, respect, shared decision
Timely
Is a delay causing harm or frustration?
Rapid stroke triage; reducing ED boarding time
wait, delay, door-to-needle
Efficient
Are supplies, equipment, energy, or ideas wasted?
Stocking carts so opened kits are not discarded; eliminating duplicate documentation
waste, cost, duplication
Equitable
Does quality vary by gender, ethnicity, location, or income?
Interpreter services; equal pain management across racial groups; rural telehealth
disparity, regardless of, all groups

check.q: A unit stops sending routine daily chest x-rays on stable post-op clients because evidence shows no benefit. Which aim is best supported, and why is “efficient” the weaker choice?
check.a: Effective, because the change is driven by evidence that the service does not benefit these clients (avoiding overuse). Cost savings follow, but the defining reason is evidence of benefit, which is the effective aim.

sections.heading: National players and the three major nursing quality efforts
sections.body:
Major organizations driving quality include the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), the American Medical Association (AMA), and the American Nurses Association (ANA). For nursing, three efforts stand out. (1) The National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators (NDNQI) collects nursing-sensitive measures, such as falls with injury, hospital-acquired pressure injuries, CAUTI, and RN skill mix, so a unit can compare itself with similar units nationally. If a manager asks, “How does our fall rate compare with other medical-surgical units our size?”, the NDNQI is the tool. (2) Patient Safety and Quality: An Evidence-Based Handbook for Nurses (AHRQ) gathers the evidence on what nurses can do to prevent harm. (3) The National Patient Safety Goals (NPSGs) from The Joint Commission are specific, annually updated requirements that accredited organizations must meet.

The NPSGs are the most bedside-relevant of the three, because many NCLEX safety items are really NPSG items in disguise. You do not need to memorize the goal numbers; you need to recognize the behavior each goal requires.

rows: Identify clients correctly
Use at least two identifiers (such as name and date of birth), never room number; match the client to the order, the medication, or the blood product.
Improve staff communication
Report critical test results to the responsible provider promptly; use read-back for verbal and telephone orders and critical values.
Use medicines safely
Label all medications and syringes off the sterile field; take extra care with anticoagulants; reconcile medications at admission, transfer, and discharge.
Use alarms safely
Respond to clinical alarms; do not silence or disable without assessing the client.
Prevent infection
Perform hand hygiene per CDC/WHO guidelines; follow bundles to prevent CLABSI, CAUTI, and surgical site infection.
Identify safety risks
Screen for suicide risk in at-risk clients and keep the environment safe.
Prevent mistakes in surgery
Verify the procedure, mark the site, and take a time-out before the procedure (Universal Protocol).

sections.example: A nurse is about to hang packed red blood cells. The client says, “You know me, I’ve been here all week.” The quality-driven action is still to ask the client to state full name and date of birth and to compare them with the wristband and the blood bank label with a second qualified verifier. Familiarity is how wrong-client transfusions happen.

sections.heading: The ACA, readmissions, bundled payments, and state roles
sections.body:
The Affordable Care Act (2010) expanded and reformed Medicaid and Medicare and tied money to quality. It created incentives to reduce 30-day readmissions (hospitals with excess readmissions for conditions such as heart failure, pneumonia, and myocardial infarction lose part of their Medicare payment) and incentives to reduce wasteful spending. After implementation, 30-day readmission rates for Medicare clients fell by more than 1% and health care-associated complications declined. That is why your discharge teaching is now a quality measure: a client who goes home not understanding daily weights or medication changes is a likely readmission.

Bundled payments pay one amount for an entire episode, such as a knee replacement and its recovery period. If the client develops an infection, falls, or is readmitted, the organization absorbs the cost. Bundles have reduced costs especially for orthopedic procedures, and they reward exactly what nurses do well: preoperative education, early mobility, complication prevention, discharge planning that begins on admission, and clean handoffs to home health or rehabilitation.

States share responsibility for health insurance programs for low-income individuals and families (Medicaid) and may create a federally subsidized Basic Health Program (BHP) for low-income adults and lawfully present immigrants. During the COVID-19 pandemic (2020), CMS and other federal agencies temporarily paused quality data reporting requirements and paused using quality data as a condition of payment, so that organizations could focus on the emergency. The point: quality reporting is powerful enough that pausing it was a national policy decision.
sections.example: A client with heart failure is being discharged. To support the readmission goal, the nurse uses teach-back for daily weights and the low-sodium diet, confirms the client can obtain the new medications, schedules a follow-up visit within 7 days, and documents that a follow-up phone call is arranged. Each action targets a known reason for return visits.

check.q: Why does a bundled payment for hip replacement give nurses a direct stake in preventing surgical site infection?
check.a: Because the single payment covers the whole episode; any complication or readmission adds cost the organization cannot bill separately, so preventing complications is both a quality and a financial priority.

sections.heading: The AHRQ National Quality Strategy: three aims, six priorities
sections.body:
The AHRQ National Quality Strategy organizes the national effort around three broad aims: Better Care (more reliable, accessible, person-centered care), Healthy People/Healthy Communities (address the behavioral, social, and environmental determinants of health), and Affordable Care (reduce cost for individuals, families, employers, and government). These aims are pursued through Box 50.1’s six priorities. When an item describes a project and asks which priority it supports, ask what the project is trying to fix.

How to sort a project in three steps. First, name the problem the project fixes (harm from care, ignored family wishes, poor communication between settings, preventable disease, unhealthy community habits, or cost). Second, match that problem to one priority in the table. Third, if two priorities seem to fit, choose the one that describes the project’s main mechanism, not a side benefit; almost every good project saves money or prevents harm somewhere, but only one priority describes how it works.

headers: What it looks like on a unit or in a community
rows: 1. Patient safety (reduce harm caused in the delivery of care)
Hand hygiene audits, CLABSI bundles, fall prevention rounds
2. Person- and family-centered care
Family presence policies, shared care-planning, bedside shift report with the client
3. Care coordination (effective communication and coordination)
Structured handoff from hospital to home health; medication reconciliation at discharge
4. Effective prevention and treatment (starting with cardiovascular disease)
Blood pressure control programs, aspirin/statin use when indicated
5. Healthy living (best practices in communities)
Smoking cessation classes, community nutrition and activity programs
6. Affordability
Reducing duplicate tests, bundled payments, reducing avoidable readmissions

check.q: A home health agency starts weekly phone calls in which a nurse reviews new medications with clients discharged from the hospital and sends a summary to the primary care office. Which National Quality Strategy priority does this most directly support, and why is “patient safety” the weaker choice?
check.a: Care coordination, because the defining purpose is communication and continuity between settings (hospital, home health, primary care). It also prevents harm, but its mechanism is coordinating information across providers; patient safety projects target harm in the delivery of care itself, such as infection bundles or fall prevention.

sections.heading: Core measures, indicators, and a culture of safety
sections.body:
Quality programs track key indicators such as infection rates, fall rates, and pressure injury incidence. Core measures are standardized clinical benchmarks for specific conditions; for example, whether a client with a stroke or myocardial infarction leaves with the evidence-based discharge medications and follow-up. When you complete discharge medication reconciliation for a client with an MI, you are feeding a core measure.

Data are only as good as staff willingness to report problems. Facilities use the AHRQ Patient Safety Culture Survey to learn whether staff feel comfortable reporting errors and near misses, whether they believe reporting leads to change, and whether they fear punishment. A low score on “nonpunitive response to error” is a red flag: if nurses hide near misses, the organization cannot see the system weaknesses that will eventually cause harm. The management response is not to demand more reports or to discipline nonreporters; it is to make reporting safe and to show staff that reports lead to fixes (topic 3 develops this into Just Culture).

check.q: A survey shows most nurses would not report a near miss for fear of being written up. What is the best first leadership action?
check.a: Establish a nonpunitive reporting process and visibly share system improvements that resulted from reports, so staff see reporting as safe and useful.

sections.heading: Ethics, informatics, and legal issues: how related concepts protect quality
sections.body:
Quality connects to several other nursing concepts. The table summarizes the relationships the source emphasizes, along with what they mean for your practice.

Ethics. Every client has the right to the best quality of care regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or ability to pay. Nurses advocate against disparities and provide culturally competent care. Patient-centered care does not mean doing anything requested: nurses also recognize preferences that are not ethical to honor, such as a parent’s refusal of a lifesaving blood transfusion for a child. (An adult with decision-making capacity may refuse a transfusion for themselves; the ethical problem is a surrogate refusing lifesaving care for a minor, which typically triggers provider, ethics, and legal involvement.)

Informatics. EHRs used at the point of care improve continuity. Nurses must record history and diagnostic information accurately and keep records current, because QI dashboards, infection surveillance, and core-measure reports are built from your documentation. Informatics also lets organizations track HAIs and identify geographic areas that lack adequate resources.

Legal issues. Consistently following federal and state laws improves quality. Be alert to abusive situations and to reckless staff behavior that risks harm or violates privacy. Ask about advance directives (living will, health care proxy, DNR orders). And avoid blaming health care workers for inadvertent mistakes; debrief and educate instead.

rows: Ethics
Clients have the right to the best quality of care.

Equal quality regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or ability to pay; advocate against disparities; cultural competence; recognize unethical preferences (e.g., refusing lifesaving blood for a child).
Informatics
EHRs at the point of care improve continuity.
Accurate, current documentation; use data to track HAIs and find under-resourced areas; protect login credentials and privacy.
Legal issues
Following federal and state law improves quality.
Watch for abuse and reckless staff behavior; ask about advance directives; protect privacy (HIPAA); debrief and educate after inadvertent errors rather than blame.

sections.example: During admission, an 80-year-old client’s daughter answers every question, and the nurse notes bruises in different stages of healing on both upper arms. The quality- and legally-sound actions are to interview the client privately, document objective findings, and report the concern through the facility process to adult protective services as required, while also asking about advance directives and who the client has chosen as health care agent.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
Several legal-quality links in this topic have specific North Carolina forms (the NCLEX is national and will not ask statute numbers, but you will practice under them).

Advance directives. NC recognizes the Health Care Power of Attorney (G.S. Chapter 32A, Article 3) and the Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death (living will, G.S. 90-321). NC’s portable medical order form is the MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment). Asking about these on admission and placing them in the record supports both legal compliance and patient-centered care.

Reporting abuse. NC is a universal reporting state for children: under G.S. 7B-301, any person or institution with cause to suspect that a juvenile (under 18) is abused, neglected, or dependent, or died from maltreatment, must report to the county department of social services (DSS) director. Report the suspicion; do not investigate or wait for proof; knowingly failing to report is a crime; good-faith reporters are immune. For disabled adults, G.S. 108A-102 requires any person with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services to report to the county DSS director, orally or in writing, with good-faith immunity.

Accountability. Nursing practice is regulated by the NC Board of Nursing (NCBON) under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.). The NCBON uses a Just Culture–based approach to practice events (covered in topic 3), which mirrors the legal-issue principle of debriefing and educating after inadvertent error rather than blaming.

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes
sections.body: Most wrong answers in this topic come from choosing a look-alike concept. Use the clue column to decide quickly.

headers: The clue that tells them apart
rows: Effective vs. Efficient
Effective = evidence-based benefit (no underuse/overuse). Efficient = no waste of supplies, equipment, time, ideas.
Stem mentions evidence or benefit → effective. Stem mentions waste, duplication, supplies → efficient.
Patient-centered vs. Equitable
Patient-centered = individual preferences and values. Equitable = same quality across groups.
One person’s choice → patient-centered. Comparison across race, language, gender, location → equitable.
Safe vs. Timely
Safe = avoid injury from care. Timely = avoid harmful delays.
Wrong drug or fall → safe. Waiting, door-to-treatment time → timely.
QI vs. Quality management
QI = continuous actions producing measurable improvement. Quality management = evaluating processes against standards to correct problems before harm and prevent over/under/misuse.
“Measurable improvement in a targeted group” → QI. “Compared with accepted standards… prevent overuse, misuse, underuse” → quality management.
NDNQI vs. NPSGs
NDNQI = comparison database of nursing-sensitive indicators. NPSGs = required safety practices from The Joint Commission.
Compare our rate with others → NDNQI. Required practice such as two identifiers → NPSG.
Core measures vs. Safety culture survey
Core measures = clinical benchmarks for conditions. Culture survey = staff perceptions about reporting and safety.
Discharge meds for MI → core measure. “Do staff feel safe reporting?” → culture survey.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: quality aims and national initiatives
sections.body:
Expect three patterns. (1) Classification in disguise: “Which action by the nurse best demonstrates [aim/goal]?” The options are all reasonable nursing actions; only one directly addresses the defining problem of that aim. (2) Systems-thinking communication: a new nurse, student, or family member says something about error or quality, and you choose the response (or identify the statement that needs further teaching) that reflects systems thinking, evidence, and client rights. (3) Initiative-to-action: the stem names a measure (readmissions, falls, CLABSI, core measure) and asks which nursing intervention most directly improves it. The correct answer targets the mechanism of the measure.

Sample question: A hospital’s quality report shows that Spanish-speaking clients on a surgical unit are reassessed after pain medication less often than English-speaking clients. Which action by the nurse manager most directly addresses the IOM aim this finding violates? (A) Survey clients about their preferred pain rating scale. (B) Ensure qualified interpreter access and audit reassessment rates by language. (C) Reduce the time from pain request to medication administration. (D) Remove unused pain-scale posters to reduce clutter.
steps: Read the stem: the data compare two language groups and show different quality of the same process (pain reassessment).
Identify what is asked: the action that addresses the violated aim. Different quality between groups = equitable.
Spot cues: “Spanish-speaking vs. English-speaking” and “less often” signal a disparity, not an individual preference.
Eliminate A: asking about preferred scales is patient-centered and useful, but it does not fix the gap between groups.
Eliminate C: shortening time to medication is the timely aim; the finding is about reassessment by language.
Eliminate D: reducing clutter is about waste (efficient) and is unrelated.
Choose B: interpreter access removes the communication barrier causing the disparity, and auditing by language measures whether the gap closes (equitable care, measured).

check.q: Reusable strategy: what two questions should you ask before choosing an IOM aim?
check.a: (1) What problem does this action prevent (injury, non-evidence care, ignored values, delay, waste, or disparity)? (2) Is the focus one person’s preference or a comparison across groups? The answers point to one aim.

sections.heading: Worked case: the heart failure readmission project
sections.body: You are a staff nurse on a cardiac step-down unit. The quarterly report shows your 30-day heart failure readmission rate is above the national benchmark, and the hospital is losing Medicare payments. The manager asks you to join a project. Three clients illustrate the problem: Mr. A did not know he should call for a 2-lb overnight weight gain; Ms. B could not afford her new diuretic; Mr. C, who speaks Vietnamese, received written teaching only in English. Your job is to reason from the data to nursing actions that address both the ACA incentive and the IOM aims.
steps: Recognize the measure and the incentive: 30-day readmission is an ACA-linked quality measure; reducing it is a federal and organizational priority.
Analyze each client’s cue for a root reason: knowledge gap (Mr. A), access/affordability (Ms. B), language barrier (Mr. C).
Match to aims: teach-back fixes effective teaching; financial counseling supports affordability and patient-centered planning; interpreter-delivered teaching addresses equitable care.

Generate solutions within nursing scope: teach-back on weights and symptoms, medication access check before discharge with case management, qualified interpreter and translated materials, follow-up appointment within 7 days, and a post-discharge phone call.
Coordinate care (National Quality Strategy priority): send a structured handoff to home health and the primary care office.
Document accurately in the EHR so the readmission data and core measures reflect what was done.
Evaluate: track readmission rates over the next quarter, separated by language group, and compare with the benchmark.

check.q: The team proposes keeping all heart failure clients one extra day “to be safe.” Why is this a weak QI solution?
check.a: It adds cost and exposure to hospital risks without addressing the identified causes (knowledge, access, language), so it is neither effective nor efficient and is unlikely to change readmissions.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 50 study guide, pp. 2851–2854 (sections 50.1 Improving the Quality of Healthcare; 50.2 National, Federal, State, and Local Initiatives, including Box 50.1; 50.3 Concepts Related to Quality Improvement). NPSG behaviors, read-back, teach-back, and readmission-reduction interventions are standard nursing content added because they apply these concepts.

Clarifications: (1) To Err Is Human was released by the IOM in November 1999 and published in 2000; it estimated 44,000 to 98,000 deaths per year (the source cites the upper figure). The >250,000 Johns Hopkins figure is an estimate that has been debated, but it is widely cited. (2) The IOM is now called the National Academy of Medicine (part of the National Academies). (3) The source’s example of an unethical preference, refusal of a lifesaving transfusion for a child, concerns a surrogate’s decision for a minor; an adult with capacity may lawfully refuse a transfusion for themselves. (4) The AHRQ National Quality Strategy was first released by HHS in 2011; CMS has since issued an updated National Quality Strategy, but the three aims and six priorities remain the framework taught here. (5) The NDNQI is now operated by Press Ganey; its function as a nursing-sensitive indicator database is unchanged. (6) The Joint Commission has been restructuring its accreditation requirements and, beginning in 2026, has been consolidating the NPSGs with related standards into a set of “National Performance Goals.” The bedside behaviors taught here (two client identifiers, prompt reporting of critical results, safe medication and alarm practices, hand hygiene and infection bundles, suicide-risk screening, and the Universal Protocol) remain expected, and both the course source and NCLEX-style items still use the NPSG name. If your clinical site uses the new name, the actions are the same.

mnemonics.name: STEEEP (the Six Aims)
mnemonics.text: Safe, Timely, Effective, Efficient, Equitable, Patient-centered. Pair the look-alikes: Effective = Evidence; Efficient = no wastE of stuff; Equitable = Equal across groups.

mnemonics.name: Better, Healthy, Affordable (NQS aims)
mnemonics.text: Better Care, Healthy People/Healthy Communities, Affordable Care, carried out through six priorities: Safety, Person/family-centered, Coordination, Prevention/treatment (CVD first), Healthy living, Affordability.

pearls: Quality includes communication, shared decision-making, and cultural sensitivity, not just technical skill.
Most errors are system failures; the best response to an error is to report it and fix the process.
Effective = evidence/benefit; efficient = waste. When a stem cites evidence, choose effective.
Equitable care compares groups; patient-centered care honors one person’s values.
Two identifiers, never a room number, every time: familiarity is not identification.
Discharge teaching with teach-back and follow-up is a readmission-reduction (quality) intervention.
Your documentation is the raw data for core measures and infection surveillance; accuracy is a quality act.
redFlags: Staff hiding near misses or saying “we don’t report that here” signals a weak safety culture and future harm.
A client or family member answering every question while the client has unexplained injuries requires a private assessment and reporting per law.
A surrogate refusing lifesaving treatment for a minor requires immediate provider and ethics/legal escalation, not silent acceptance.
Copy-forward or delayed documentation corrupts quality data and can hide deterioration.
A measurable gap in care between language or racial groups is an equity problem the nurse should report and help fix.
recap: Quality = care that increases the likelihood of desired outcomes and matches current knowledge.
QI = systematic, continuous actions producing measurable improvement; quality management compares processes to standards to prevent harm and misuse of resources.
To Err Is Human shifted focus to systems; Crossing the Quality Chasm set the Six Aims (STEEEP).
Three nursing efforts: NDNQI, AHRQ evidence-based handbook for nurses, and Joint Commission NPSGs.
The ACA tied payment to quality, especially 30-day readmissions; bundled payments reward coordinated episodes of care.
AHRQ NQS: three aims and six priorities guide national projects.
Ethics, informatics, and law all support quality: equal care, accurate records, advance directives, abuse reporting, and debriefing rather than blaming.

checks.q: A nurse rearranges a supply room so that sterile kits no longer expire unused. Which aim is this, and what makes it different from the effective aim?
checks.a: Efficient. It prevents waste of supplies; it is not about whether a treatment is evidence-based or beneficial.

checks.q: A client tells the nurse she prefers to shower in the evening because of her religious practice. The nurse adjusts the schedule. Which aim does this demonstrate?
checks.a: Patient-centered care, because the client’s values and preferences are guiding the plan.

checks.q: Your unit wants to know whether its CAUTI rate is better or worse than similar hospitals. Which resource fits best, and why not the NPSGs?
checks.a: The NDNQI, because it is a comparison database of nursing-sensitive indicators; the NPSGs are required safety practices, not a benchmarking database.

checks.q: Which nursing action most directly supports the ACA readmission goal for a client with COPD being discharged?
checks.a: Teach-back of inhaler technique and action plan, confirming medication access, and arranging early follow-up; these target the common causes of return visits.

checks.q: A colleague gives a medication 2 hours late because of an emergency on the unit and no harm results. What does the legal-issues row of QI recommend?
checks.a: Report the event through the facility system and debrief and educate about workflow rather than blame the nurse for an inadvertent mistake.

checks.q: A father refuses a lifesaving transfusion for his 7-year-old. What is the nurse’s priority role?
checks.a: Advocate for the child by promptly notifying the provider and engaging ethics/legal resources per policy, while communicating respectfully with the family; the nurse does not transfuse without a valid order and authority, nor ignore the refusal.

topics.title: The QI Process, Measurement (Donabedian) & Quality Management Programs
topics.summary: QI is a continuous cycle: analyze current care (peer review, audits, outcomes and utilization review), compare it with benchmarks using structure, process, and outcome indicators, test changes (PDSA, CQI, TQM, Six Sigma, Lean), and confirm results with quality assurance.
objectives: Describe the QI process as a continuous, multistep, multilevel cycle and distinguish QI from performance improvement.
Differentiate intraprofessional from interprofessional assessment and classify peer review, audits, outcomes management, and utilization review.
Distinguish retrospective from concurrent audits and choose the right one for a given QI question.
Classify indicators as structure, process, or outcome using the Donabedian model and NDNQI Box 50.2, and judge whether a proposed indicator is measurable, objective, and sensitive.
Interpret benchmark comparisons to select an area for improvement.
Sequence the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle and identify the phase a team is in.
Compare quality assurance, TQM, CQI, Six Sigma, and Lean and match each to a described project.
topics.bigPicture:
Topic 1 told you what quality is. This topic is about how an organization finds out whether it is delivering it and how it gets better. QI is not a one-time project; it is a loop. A team looks at what is happening now (chart audits, peer review, client-reported outcomes), compares it with a benchmark, picks a gap, tests a change on a small scale, studies the results, and either adopts the change or tries again. Then quality assurance checks that the gains hold.

Staff nurses are central to every step. You are the person whose charting is audited, whose peers review your care against standards, who pilots the new hourly rounding script, and who notices that the new process is not working at 3 a.m. Understanding the vocabulary lets you participate meaningfully instead of feeling that QI is something done to you.

NCLEX items here are usually classification-with-a-scenario (“Which type of audit is this?”, “Which indicator measures a process?”), sequencing (“Which PDSA step comes next?”), or judgment (“Which indicator is most appropriate?”, “Which result should the team target first?”). The skill is reading the scenario for the clue words that place it in the right box.

keyTerms.def: A continuous, multistep, multilevel process that identifies areas for improvement based on performance and industry standards.
QI that is directly linked to the performance of an individual, team, unit, or organization.

Assessment carried out within a group of individuals who hold similar positions in a health care system (for example, a group of nurses or a group of surgeons); includes peer reviews, audits, and outcomes management.
Professional critique of a colleague’s work, based on predetermined standards, in a safe, nonpunitive environment.
An examination of records to verify accuracy and proper use; intraprofessional if focused on one discipline, interprofessional if focused on several disciplines.
Audit performed after a client’s discharge that compares care provided to one client with care provided to similar clients.
Audit performed while the client is still receiving care that evaluates the adequacy of ongoing nursing care so adverse events can be prevented in real time.
Use of client experiences to guide improvement by linking medical interventions, health outcomes, and cost of care.
NIH Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System; standardized tools that measure physical, mental, and social well-being from the client’s perspective.
Collaborative assessment among providers from multiple disciplines (for example, surgeon, physician, nurse, dietitian, physical therapist).

Analysis of resource use to identify overuse, misuse, and underuse (for example, unnecessary urinary catheters in incontinent ambulatory clients, or inadequate staffing); required for Medicare/Medicaid participation and by accreditors.
Comparing the performance of an individual or organization with industry standards (established models of high-quality performance from the ANA, specialty organizations, or clinical research).
Avedis Donabedian’s framework linking quality standards to three dimensions: structure, process, and outcome.
Standards about material resources, human resources, and organizational structure: the capacity and systems for providing care (staffing, equipment, certification).
Standards about the steps used to reach an outcome: whether the required steps exist and are followed (for example, fall-risk assessment completed on admission).
Standards about the results of care (for example, the number of bedridden clients who develop a pressure injury).
A statistic that reflects an organization’s performance in a specific area so it can be compared with industry standards; must be measurable, objective, and sensitive to changes in performance.
Structure, process, and outcome measures that reflect nursing care (e.g., skill mix, falls, pressure injuries, CAUTI, CLABSI).
Evaluation of implemented changes by collecting post-intervention data and comparing them with benchmark standards to determine whether standards are met; if not, QI continues.

A plan that integrates new programs, models, and technologies with existing primary care services across clinical, managerial, administrative, and facility aspects; addresses engagement, population health, and value (per capita cost) and uses client satisfaction surveys and follow-up.

Comprehensive management philosophy rooted in Walter Shewhart’s work and made famous by W. Edwards Deming; relies on organization-wide teamwork (including suppliers and customers), communication, feedback, fact-based decisions, and continual improvement.

Deming’s modification of Shewhart’s Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle: plan a change and predictions, do it on a small scale, study the data against predictions, and act by adapting, adopting, or abandoning the change.

Customer-driven, progressive, incremental improvement applied to specific problems, policies and procedures, resource use, and EBP; serves internal customers (staff) and external customers (clients, families, payers).
Data-driven quality program that reduces defects and variation in a process (classically using Define-Measure-Analyze-Improve-Control).
Lean removes workflow waste (steps that add no value); Lean Six Sigma combines waste removal with defect and variation reduction to improve safety and efficiency.

sections.heading: QI is a loop, not a project
sections.body: The QI process is continuous, multistep, and multilevel: it identifies areas for improvement by comparing actual performance with performance standards and industry standards. When QI is tied directly to how well an individual, team, unit, or organization performs, it is called performance improvement. The steps below follow the module’s sequence. Keep the loop in mind: the last step (QA) feeds back into the first whenever standards are not met.
steps: Analyze current protocols and outcomes: intraprofessional assessment (peer review, audits, outcomes management), interprofessional assessment, and utilization review.
Benchmark: compare performance with industry standards using Donabedian structure, process, and outcome indicators.
Target areas for improvement: prioritize gaps, sentinel events, breaches of care, and risk-management findings (topic 3).
Identify factors that promote better outcomes: root cause analysis, medication safety, staffing, resource use, Just Culture, and EBP (topic 3).
Implement and test changes using a quality program (PDSA, CQI, TQM, Six Sigma, Lean).
Evaluate with quality assurance: collect post-intervention data, compare with the benchmark, and continue QI if the standard is not met.
sections.analogy: QI works like a thermostat. It measures the room (audit), compares it with the set point (benchmark), turns on the heat if it is cold (intervention), and keeps measuring (QA). A thermostat that measured once and then shut off would not keep the house warm.

sections.heading: Intraprofessional assessment: peer review and outcomes management
sections.body:
Intraprofessional means within one profession (intra = inside): nurses reviewing nurses, surgeons reviewing surgeons. It includes peer review, audits, and outcomes management.

Peer review is a colleague’s professional critique of your work against predetermined standards in a safe, nonpunitive environment. Three features make it peer review: the reviewers are peers (similar role and level), the standards are set in advance, and the purpose is learning and improvement rather than punishment. A manager writing a disciplinary note is not peer review; neither is a client satisfaction survey.

Outcomes management uses client experiences to guide improvement by linking interventions, health outcomes, and cost. A common tool is the NIH’s PROMIS, which measures physical, mental, and social well-being as reported by the client. For example, an orthopedic clinic might compare PROMIS physical-function scores 6 weeks after two different post-op mobility protocols and their costs.
sections.example: Clinical Exemplar A. Mrs. Ruth Davison, 74, had a carpal tunnel repair. She misunderstood her discharge instructions and removed her surgical dressing after 1 day instead of 2, then reported slight bleeding and redness. This triggered an intraprofessional assessment: the two RNs who cared for her, two additional RNs, and the nurse manager reviewed her chart, compared it with similar cases, and followed up with Mrs. Davison to evaluate how clear the discharge teaching was and how satisfied she was. Note that the immediate clinical priority when she called was to assess the wound (amount of bleeding, signs of infection, sensation and movement of the hand) and give appropriate care instructions; the QI review addresses why the teaching failed so it does not happen to the next client. Likely fixes include plain-language written instructions with the removal date, teach-back, and a follow-up call.

check.q: Why is the Davison review intraprofessional even though it involved a manager?
check.a: All reviewers were nurses (staff RNs and the nurse manager), so the assessment stayed within one discipline; adding a surgeon or occupational therapist would make it interprofessional.

sections.heading: Audits: retrospective vs. concurrent, intra vs. inter
sections.body:
An audit examines records to verify accuracy and proper use. Two separate questions classify any audit. When? A retrospective audit happens after discharge and compares one client’s care with that of similar clients. A concurrent audit happens while the client is still receiving care and checks whether ongoing care is adequate so adverse events can be prevented in real time. Who? An audit of one discipline (nursing documentation) is intraprofessional; an audit of several disciplines (nursing and medical documentation of sepsis care) is interprofessional.

Choose the audit by the purpose. If the goal is to catch a missed fall-risk intervention before a client falls tonight, only a concurrent audit can do that. If the goal is to learn whether discharge teaching for all hip-fracture clients last quarter met the standard, a retrospective audit fits.

rows: Timing
After discharge
During the stay
Main purpose
Compare care with similar clients; find patterns
Evaluate ongoing care; prevent harm now
Can it change this client’s care?
No (client has left)
Yes
Typical method
Closed chart review
Open chart review, observation, client interview
Example
Reviewing last quarter’s charts for discharge teaching on anticoagulants
Daily check that every client with a central line has a dated dressing and a documented line-necessity review

check.q: A nurse manager walks the unit each morning to confirm that clients on restraints have documented circulation checks. What kind of audit is this?
check.a: A concurrent (intraprofessional, if only nursing care is reviewed) audit, because it evaluates care while clients are still receiving it so problems can be corrected immediately.

sections.heading: Interprofessional assessment and utilization review
sections.body:
Interprofessional (interdisciplinary) assessment involves collaboration among several disciplines, such as a surgeon, physician, nurse, dietitian, and physical therapist reviewing why post-op clients are developing prolonged ileus. Problems that cross professional boundaries (nutrition, mobility, medication, discharge) need interprofessional review, because no single discipline can see or fix the whole process.

Utilization review analyzes how resources are used to find overuse, misuse, and underuse. Overuse: indwelling urinary catheters placed in incontinent clients who can walk to the bathroom (unnecessary, and a CAUTI risk). Underuse: inadequate staffing, or failing to give evidence-based VTE prophylaxis. Misuse: an appropriate service is provided, but a preventable complication occurs because it was delivered incorrectly, such as an indicated anticoagulant given at the wrong dose, or a needed IV line that infiltrates because it was not monitored. (Ordering an expensive scan when a simpler test answers the question is usually classed as overuse.) Utilization review is required for hospitals that participate in Medicare and Medicaid and is expected by The Joint Commission.

The nursing response to a utilization finding is usually a protocol or practice change within nursing scope: for the catheter example, a nurse-driven protocol to review catheter indications daily and remove catheters that no longer meet criteria, bladder scanning, and scheduled toileting.
sections.example: A utilization review finds that clients on a medical unit stay an average of 1.5 days longer than benchmark because physical therapy evaluations are ordered late. An interprofessional team (hospitalist, RN, PT, case manager) agrees that nurses will screen mobility on admission and trigger PT consults by protocol. This is utilization review (finding overuse of hospital days caused by late use of a needed service) feeding interprofessional assessment and a process change.

check.q: Classify each utilization finding as overuse, underuse, or misuse: (a) daily CBCs on stable clients with no indication; (b) eligible surgical clients not receiving VTE prophylaxis; (c) an ordered insulin drip running at the wrong rate and causing hypoglycemia.
check.a: (a) Overuse: a service given when it is not likely to benefit. (b) Underuse: a beneficial service not provided. (c) Misuse: an appropriate service delivered incorrectly, causing a preventable complication.

sections.heading: Benchmarking and indicators: how do we know we are good?
sections.body:
Benchmarking compares an individual’s or organization’s performance with industry standards: established models of high-quality performance from the ANA, specialty organizations, or clinical research, and comparison data such as the NDNQI. A benchmark turns “we seem to have a lot of falls” into “our injury-fall rate is 1.2 per 1,000 patient days versus 0.6 for similar units.”

An indicator is the statistic used for that comparison. Good indicators are measurable (can be counted or calculated), objective (two people would get the same number), and sensitive to changes in performance (if care improves, the number moves). “Staff feel infection care is better” fails all three. “CLABSIs per 1,000 central-line days” passes: it is countable, defined, and adjusts for how many lines were in use, so it responds to real change.

When a report shows several indicators against benchmarks, the usual priority is the indicator with the largest unfavorable gap that reflects client harm, especially if it is trending worse. An indicator that is better than benchmark is maintained, not targeted.

check.q: Your unit’s CAUTI rate is 2.8 per 1,000 catheter days (benchmark 1.0); falls are 2.1 per 1,000 patient days (benchmark 2.5). Which should be targeted first and why?
check.a: CAUTI, because it is nearly three times the benchmark and reflects client harm; falls are already better than benchmark and should be maintained.

sections.heading: The Donabedian model: structure, process, outcome
sections.body:
Avedis Donabedian proposed that quality can be judged in three linked dimensions. Structure is the capacity to give care: material resources (beds, lifts, equipment), human resources (staffing, skill mix, certification, education), and organizational structure. Process is what is done and how: whether required steps exist and are followed. Outcome is the result for the client: the number of bedridden clients who develop a pressure injury, infection rates, readmissions.

The logic runs left to right: good structure makes good process possible, and good process makes good outcomes more likely. When outcomes are poor, look backward: is the process being followed, and does the structure support it? A pressure injury outcome problem might trace to a turning process that is not being followed, which might trace to a structure problem (not enough staff or no pressure-redistribution mattresses).

Box 50.2 places NDNQI nursing-sensitive indicators into these categories. Note that some (falls, pressure injuries, pain impairing function) are measured as both process and outcome: the process measure is whether prevention was done (fall-risk assessment, prevention plan), and the outcome measure is whether the event happened.

rows: Structure
Capacity: people, equipment, organization
Nursing turnover; RN education and certification; nursing skill mix; admissions/discharges/transfers; ED throughput; workforce characteristics; patient contacts; patient volume and flow
Process
Whether the right steps are done
Pediatric pain assessment-intervention-reassessment (AIR) cycles; care coordination; device utilization; pain impairing function*; patient falls*; pressure injuries*; restraint use
Outcome
Results for clients (and staff)

CAUTI; CLABSI; hospital readmissions; MDROs; C. difficile and MRSA infections; ventilator-associated events and pneumonia; unplanned post-op transfers/admissions; pediatric peripheral IV infiltrations; burns; surgical errors; assaults by psychiatric clients; assaults on nursing personnel

sections.analogy: Picture a play. Structure is the stage, the lights, and the cast (resources). Process is the performance: are the actors saying the right lines in the right order? Outcome is the review in the morning paper. A great review needs both a working stage and a good performance.

check.q: Classify: (a) percentage of RNs with specialty certification, (b) percentage of clients with a fall-risk assessment within 24 hours of admission, (c) falls with injury per 1,000 patient days.
check.a: (a) structure, (b) process, (c) outcome.

sections.heading: Quality assurance and the quality management programs
sections.body:
Quality assurance (QA) evaluates changes after they are implemented: the team collects post-intervention data and compares them with benchmark standards to see whether standards are met. If they are not, QI continues. QA answers “Did it work, and is it holding?” A comprehensive quality management plan integrates new programs, models, and technologies with existing primary care services across clinical, managerial, administrative, and facility aspects; it addresses engagement, population health, and value (per capita cost) and uses client satisfaction surveys and follow-up.

Organizations choose a program or model to structure the work. TQM is a whole-organization philosophy: everyone, including suppliers and customers, shares responsibility for quality, with communication, feedback, fact-based decisions, and continual improvement. PDSA is the small-test-of-change engine, Deming’s modification of Shewhart’s PDCA. CQI is customer-driven, incremental improvement applied to specific problems, policies, resource use, and EBP; its customers are internal (nurses, physicians, therapists, medical records, billing) and external (clients, families, payers). Six Sigma uses data to eliminate defects and variation; Lean removes waste (non-value-added steps); Lean Six Sigma combines both.

How to identify the program in a stem. Ask three questions in order. (1) Is the team checking results after a change against a standard? That is QA. (2) Is the team running a small, time-limited test with predictions? That is PDSA. (3) What is the team trying to eliminate? Defects and variation point to Six Sigma; wasted steps, walking, and waiting point to Lean; and when the stem describes a whole-organization philosophy in which everyone, including suppliers and customers, owns quality, it is TQM. CQI is the answer when the stem stresses ongoing, incremental, customer-driven improvement of a specific problem and names internal or external customers.

headers: How you recognize it in a stem
rows: TQM
Shewhart roots; made famous by Deming; organization-wide philosophy
Everyone in the organization, suppliers and customers included, owns quality; fact-based decisions
PDSA
Deming’s modification of Shewhart’s PDCA; linked to TQM
Small-scale test, predictions, data compared with predictions, then adopt/adapt/abandon
CQI
Customer-driven, progressive incremental improvement
Ongoing small improvements to a specific problem; internal and external customers
Six Sigma
Data-driven defect and variation reduction
Reduce errors/variation in a process; statistical measurement; DMAIC
Lean
Waste removal in workflow
Map steps, eliminate non-value-added steps, walking, waiting, duplication
QA
Post-implementation evaluation
Compare post-change data with the benchmark; are standards met?

check.q: One team maps every step from a blood-product order to the start of the transfusion and removes steps that add no value. Six months after a new CAUTI bundle, a different team compares infection data with the benchmark. Name the program or activity in each case.
check.a: The first is Lean (removing non-value-added steps and waste from a workflow). The second is quality assurance (comparing post-intervention data with the benchmark to see whether the standard is met; if not, QI continues).

sections.heading: PDSA step by step
sections.body: PDSA is the most testable program because its phases are sequential and each has distinct activities. The key is that the test is small (one unit, one shift, a few clients) and the team makes predictions in advance so the Study phase has something to compare with.
steps: Plan: define the objective; state predictions (what you expect to happen and why); decide who, what, where, and when; and plan how data will be collected.
Do: carry out the plan on a small scale; document observations and problems; record data.
Study: analyze the data; compare results with predictions; summarize what was learned.
Act: decide what changes are needed (adopt, adapt, or abandon); plan the next cycle; adopt organization-wide if the goal was met.
sections.example: A team predicts that hourly purposeful rounding will reduce call-light use and falls by 25% on one unit over 4 weeks (Plan). Night shift nurses round hourly and record the time and needs addressed (Do). After 4 weeks, falls dropped 30% but rounding compliance was only 60% at 3–5 a.m. (Study). The team adapts the script for night shift and runs a second cycle before spreading to other units (Act).

check.q: A team has piloted bedside shift report on one unit for a month and has collected satisfaction and handoff-error data. What is the next PDSA step?
check.a: Study: analyze the data and compare the results with the predictions made in the Plan phase before deciding whether to adopt the change.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
Under the NC Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.) and the NCBON rules on RN components of practice (21 NCAC 36 .0224), the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. QI work fits naturally into the evaluation component: the RN evaluates whether client outcomes are met and revises the plan. The LPN participates under RN or provider supervision (21 NCAC 36 .0225).

In a QI project, unlicensed assistive personnel (Nurse Aide I or II) may collect simple data within their approved task list, such as recording the time of hourly rounds or counting call lights, but the RN interprets the data, evaluates client responses, and judges whether the plan should change. The RN may delegate tasks, not the nursing process or judgment. Peer review in NC organizations is designed to be educational and nonpunitive; conduct issues (such as impairment, diversion, or falsification) are handled through reporting to the NCBON rather than through peer review alone.

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes
sections.body: The classification items in this topic are won or lost on single words. Use this table to train your eye.

headers: The clue that tells them apart
rows: Intraprofessional vs. Interprofessional
Intra = within one discipline; inter = several disciplines.
Count the professions in the stem: all nurses → intra; RN + MD + RD + PT → inter.
Retrospective vs. Concurrent audit
Retrospective = after discharge; concurrent = during care.
“Discharged,” “last quarter,” “closed charts” → retrospective. “Currently admitted,” “in real time,” “prevent now” → concurrent.
Peer review vs. Performance appraisal
Peer review = colleagues, predetermined standards, nonpunitive. Appraisal/discipline = manager evaluation.
Who reviews and whether the tone is punitive.
Structure vs. Process indicator
Structure = resources/capacity; process = steps done.
Counts of staff, certifications, equipment → structure. “Percentage of clients who received…” → process.
Process vs. Outcome indicator
Process = was prevention done; outcome = did the event occur.
“Assessed,” “documented,” “received” → process. “Developed,” “infection rate,” “readmitted” → outcome.
QA vs. QI
QA = check post-intervention data against the benchmark; QI = the continuous improvement work.
“After implementation, compare with the standard” → QA.
Six Sigma vs. Lean
Six Sigma = defects/variation; Lean = waste/non-value steps.
Error rates, variation, statistical control → Six Sigma. Walking, waiting, duplicate steps → Lean.
Utilization review vs. Outcomes management
UR = overuse, misuse, underuse of resources; outcomes management = links interventions, outcomes, and cost using client experiences (PROMIS).
Resource appropriateness → UR. Client-reported well-being → outcomes management.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: classifying QI activities and sequencing PDSA
sections.body:
Common patterns: (1) “Which type of review/audit/indicator is this?” with a short scenario; (2) “Which indicator would best measure…?” requiring the measurable-objective-sensitive test; (3) exhibit items showing unit data against benchmarks and asking what to target or what to conclude; (4) “Which PDSA step is next?” or “Which activity belongs in the Plan phase?”; (5) “Which statement by the nurse indicates a need for further teaching about peer review/QA?”

Sample question: A QI team wants to know whether the new sepsis screening tool is being used for every client admitted through the ED. Which indicator is most appropriate? (A) Sepsis mortality rate on the medical unit. (B) Percentage of ED admissions with a completed sepsis screen within 1 hour of arrival. (C) Number of RNs trained to use the sepsis tool. (D) Nurses’ ratings of how easy the tool is to use.
steps: Read the stem: the question is whether the tool is being used, which is a question about steps of care.
Identify what is asked: an indicator of a process (Donabedian), and one that is measurable, objective, and sensitive.
Eliminate A: mortality is an outcome; it is influenced by many factors and does not tell you whether screening was done.
Eliminate C: number trained is a structure measure (capacity), not actual use.
Eliminate D: satisfaction ratings are subjective and do not measure completion.
Choose B: it is a process indicator, countable, objective, time-defined, and it will move if use improves.

check.q: Reusable strategy for indicator items?
check.a: First match the indicator type to the question (resources → structure, steps → process, results → outcome); then test it for measurable, objective, and sensitive. Reject feelings, totals without a denominator, and measures of a different dimension.

sections.heading: Worked case: reducing falls on an orthopedic unit
sections.body: You are a staff RN on a 30-bed orthopedic unit. The NDNQI report shows injury falls at 1.4 per 1,000 patient days versus a benchmark of 0.7. Process data show fall-risk assessments are documented on 95% of admissions, but bed alarms are activated for only 55% of high-risk clients at night. Structure data show night shift skill mix dropped after two RN resignations. The manager asks you to co-lead a PDSA cycle.
steps: Recognize the gap with benchmarking: the outcome indicator (injury falls) is twice the benchmark.
Analyze using Donabedian backward: outcome is poor; the assessment process is done, but the prevention process (bed alarms) is not; the structure (night skill mix) may explain why.
Select an indicator for the test: percentage of high-risk clients with an activated bed alarm on hourly night checks (process), plus injury falls (outcome).
Plan: objective = 90% alarm compliance in 4 weeks on one hallway; prediction = falls will decrease; who/what/when defined; charge nurse and UAP record alarm checks; RN reviews daily.
Do: run the test on one hallway, record data and barriers (alarms too sensitive, staff unsure who resets).
Study: compliance rose to 88%; one injury fall vs. three in the comparison month; staff report confusion over reset responsibility.

Act: adapt by assigning alarm reset to the assigned RN/UAP pair and adding it to hourly rounding; run a second cycle, then spread unit-wide; escalate the night skill-mix issue to the manager as a structure problem.
Evaluate with QA: after spread, compare the unit’s injury-fall rate with the benchmark quarterly; if still above, continue QI.

check.q: Why did the team not simply repeat fall-risk education about documentation?
check.a: Because the process data showed assessment documentation was already 95%; the gap was in the prevention step and the structure supporting it. Fix the step that is failing, not the one that is working.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 50 study guide, pp. 2854–2856 (50.4 steps 1–2: analysis of current protocols, intraprofessional and interprofessional assessment, peer review, audits, outcomes management, utilization review, Clinical Exemplar A, benchmarking, Donabedian model, indicators; Box 50.2) and pp. 2859–2860 (50.5 Quality Management Programs: QA, comprehensive quality management plan, TQM, PDSA, CQI, Six Sigma and Lean Six Sigma, high-yield comparisons).

Clarifications: (1) The source says TQM was “invented by Walter Shewhart.” More precisely, Shewhart developed statistical process control and the Plan-Do-Check cycle that underlie TQM; Deming (with others such as Juran) developed and popularized TQM as a management philosophy. (2) Utilization review is required by the CMS Conditions of Participation for hospitals in Medicare and Medicaid; the source’s wording “required by Medicaid and The Joint Commission” is kept in spirit. (3) DMAIC and the description of Lean as waste removal are standard additions to the brief Six Sigma entry. (4) In Exemplar A, the source focuses on the QI review; the guide adds that the immediate clinical step when the client called was a wound assessment, consistent with assess-before-act.

mnemonics.name: SPO = Stage, Performance, Outcome (Donabedian)
mnemonics.text: Structure is the stage and cast (resources, staffing, certification); Process is the performance (steps done); Outcome is the review (what happened to the client).

mnemonics.name: PDSA = Predict, Do small, Study vs. prediction, Act (adopt/adapt/abandon)
mnemonics.text: If the team is still predicting and planning data collection, it is Plan; if it is running the test, Do; if it is comparing results with predictions, Study; if it is deciding to spread or change, Act.

mnemonics.name: Intra = Inside one profession; Inter = Interacting professions
mnemonics.text: All nurses → intraprofessional; nurse + surgeon + dietitian + PT → interprofessional.

pearls: Concurrent audits can still help the current client; retrospective audits cannot.
Peer review is nonpunitive and uses predetermined standards; discipline is not peer review.
A good indicator is measurable, objective, and sensitive to change, and usually has a denominator (per 1,000 patient days, per 1,000 line days).
Falls, pressure injuries, and pain impairing function are measured as both process and outcome.
When outcomes are poor, trace backward: is the process done, and does the structure support it?
PDSA starts small and requires predictions; never adopt organization-wide before the Study phase.
QA asks whether post-change data meet the benchmark; if not, the QI loop continues.
redFlags: A concurrent audit that finds a missing safety intervention (e.g., no restraint checks) requires immediate correction for that client, not just a note for the report.
Peer review used as a punitive tool undermines reporting and safety culture.
Spreading a change unit-wide without studying pilot data can spread a harmful or ineffective process.
Indicators based on staff opinion alone can hide real deterioration in outcomes.
Utilization findings of overuse (e.g., unnecessary catheters) are also safety findings because overuse creates infection risk.
recap: QI is continuous, multistep, and multilevel; tied to a person, team, or unit it is performance improvement.
Intraprofessional assessment (peer review, audits, outcomes management) stays within one discipline; interprofessional crosses disciplines.
Retrospective audit = after discharge; concurrent audit = during care, to prevent harm now.
Utilization review finds overuse, misuse, and underuse of resources.
Benchmarking compares performance with industry standards using measurable, objective, sensitive indicators.
Donabedian: structure (capacity) → process (steps) → outcome (results).
PDSA: Plan with predictions, Do on a small scale, Study against predictions, Act to adopt/adapt/abandon.
QA checks post-intervention data against benchmarks; TQM, CQI, Six Sigma, and Lean structure the improvement work.

checks.q: A surgeon, an RN, a dietitian, and a PT review charts of clients with post-op ileus. Is this intraprofessional or interprofessional, and why does it matter?
checks.a: Interprofessional; the problem involves medical, nursing, nutrition, and mobility processes, so only a multidisciplinary review can see and fix the whole process.

checks.q: Which indicator is the outcome measure: number of wound-care certified nurses, percentage of clients turned every 2 hours, or stage 3 pressure injuries per 1,000 patient days?
checks.a: Stage 3 pressure injuries per 1,000 patient days (outcome). Certified nurses is structure; turning compliance is process.

checks.q: The team ran a pilot and now proposes adopting it across the hospital without looking at the data. What PDSA error is this?
checks.a: Skipping the Study phase; results must be analyzed and compared with predictions before deciding to adopt.

checks.q: A nurse manager says, “We will use peer review to find out who should be written up for documentation errors.” How should you respond?
checks.a: Peer review is a nonpunitive professional critique against predetermined standards to improve practice; using it for discipline defeats its purpose and discourages honest participation.

checks.q: A pharmacy-to-bedside workflow involves nurses walking to a distant med room 20 times per shift. Which quality program best fits redesigning it?
checks.a: Lean, because the problem is non-value-added waste (walking, waiting) in a workflow.

checks.q: After a new CAUTI bundle, the team collects 3 months of infection data and compares it with the NDNQI benchmark. Which activity is this?
checks.a: Quality assurance: evaluating post-intervention data against the benchmark; if the standard is not met, QI continues.

topics.title: Sentinel Events, Risk Management, Root Cause Analysis & Just Culture
topics.summary: When harm happens or nearly happens, quality depends on what the organization does next: recognize sentinel events, assess and protect the client, report, analyze root causes in systems, reduce medication and staffing risks, and respond to people fairly using Just Culture.
objectives: Identify sentinel events and explain the required response, including a credible root cause analysis (RCA2).
Define breach of care and describe the proactive and reactive components of risk management, including incident (occurrence) reporting.
Apply RCA2 principles: focus on systems, distinguish special-cause from common-cause variation, and build action plans with owners, timelines, and measures.
Differentiate a medication error from an adverse drug event, recognize high-risk medications, and select system safeguards and the correct sequence after an error.
Relate RN staffing, skill mix, and NDNQI nursing-sensitive indicators to client outcomes and resource waste.
Classify behavior as human error, at-risk behavior, or reckless behavior and choose the Just Culture response (console, coach, discipline).
Apply personal-responsibility rules and the AACN healthy work environment standards to student and new-nurse dilemmas.
topics.bigPicture:
Errors will happen in every hospital. What separates a safe organization from a dangerous one is whether errors and near misses are seen, reported, analyzed, and fixed. This topic covers the machinery that does that: the sentinel event policy that forces a deep investigation after catastrophic harm, risk management that tries to prevent harm and limit damage, root cause analysis that looks for the system weakness rather than the person to blame, and medication-safety tools such as barcode scanning and CPOE.

It also covers the human side. A culture where nurses are punished for every mistake drives errors underground. A culture where nothing has consequences tolerates reckless behavior. Just Culture threads the needle: console the person who slipped, coach the person who took a risky shortcut, and discipline the person who consciously disregarded a substantial risk. You will need to classify behavior quickly, because NCLEX items frequently ask how a charge nurse or manager should respond to a colleague’s action.

At the bedside, the rules are concrete. If you make or discover an error, assess the client first, then notify the provider, follow orders, document facts in the record, and complete an incident report. If a colleague is impaired, remove them from client care now. If you are a student asked to do something you have never done, say no and get supervision. These are some of the most reliably tested behaviors in the Safe and Effective Care Environment category.

keyTerms.def: Current Joint Commission definition: a patient safety event, not primarily related to the natural course of the client’s illness or underlying condition, that reaches the client and results in death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm. It requires immediate investigation and a comprehensive (credible) root cause analysis. Older wording in the source: an unexpected occurrence involving death or serious physical or psychological injury (including loss of limb or function), or the risk thereof.

Unanticipated death or major permanent loss of function unrelated to the original illness; invasive procedure on the wrong client, wrong site, or wrong procedure; unintended retention of a foreign object; radiation overdose or wrong body region; hemolytic transfusion reaction from incompatible blood; abduction, rape, assault, or homicide in the facility; suicide in a staffed around-the-clock setting or within 72 hours of discharge; severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia; elopement from a staffed around-the-clock setting leading to death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm.

Deviation by the nurse from the standard of care. CRICO data show nurses are most often involved in breaches around bedside care (medication administration, monitoring IVs/catheters/wounds), falls, pressure injuries, and communication breakdowns.

The clinical and administrative systems, processes, and reports used to detect, monitor, assess, mitigate, and prevent risks; it has proactive (prevent adverse events) and reactive (minimize damage after an event) components.
A major risk factor for liability; unhappy, unheard clients are more likely to file claims.
