Confidential internal report of an unusual event, error, or near miss, completed factually and sent to risk management; used for QI and is not part of the client’s medical record.
An error or unsafe event that is caught before it reaches the client; it should be reported because it reveals the same system weakness as an actual error.

“Root Cause Analysis and Action” (RCA2: Improving Root Cause Analysis and Actions to Prevent Harm): a structured investigation that focuses on systems and processes, not individual performance; analyzes special-cause and common-cause variation; and produces action plans with responsible parties, timelines, pilot testing, and effectiveness metrics.
Variation beyond what is normal for a process, usually due to a specific, identifiable change or event.
Normal, expected variation built into the system; reducing it requires redesigning the system.
Any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or client harm while the medication is in the control of the health care professional, client, or consumer.
Harm experienced by a client as a result of exposure to a medication; not all ADEs are errors (e.g., an unpredictable allergic reaction to a correctly given drug), though many are preventable.

Drugs with heightened risk of serious harm when misused, such as IV unfractionated heparin; ISMP look-alike, sound-alike (LASA) drugs; and Beers Criteria medications in adults 65 and older (e.g., benzodiazepines).
American Geriatrics Society list of potentially inappropriate medications for adults 65 and older because of increased risk (e.g., benzodiazepines, strongly anticholinergic drugs).
Barcode scanning of the client ID band and medication, tall-man lettering and regulation of similar names, pharmacy first-dose review, and Computerized Provider Order Entry (CPOE).
The proportion of total nursing hours provided by RNs; higher RN skill mix and more nursing hours are associated with fewer adverse outcomes.
Death after a complication that might have been recognized and treated in time; a nursing-sensitive outcome linked to RN staffing.

Reducing waste such as unnecessary procedures, excessive administrative costs, missed prevention, fraud, prolonged stays from medication errors, extra visits from poor client education, and lost time from poor equipment or documentation.
A setting where health care professionals can report errors or near misses without fear of punishment so system problems can be identified and fixed.

Balances a blame-free environment with appropriate accountability and zero tolerance for reckless behavior; distinguishes human error (console, fix system), at-risk behavior (coach), and reckless behavior (disciplinary action).
An inadvertent slip, lapse, or mistake: doing something other than intended. Response: console the person and fix the system.
A choice that increases risk where the risk is not recognized or is mistakenly believed justified, such as shortcuts or drifting from rules. Response: coach.
Conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk, such as working under the influence of alcohol or narcotics. Response: disciplinary action.

keyTerms.term: AACN standards for a healthy work environment
keyTerms.def: Six standards: skilled communication, true collaboration, effective decision-making, appropriate staffing, meaningful recognition, and authentic leadership.
Never perform an act you are uncertain how to perform, follow facility policies and procedures, and report errors properly.

sections.heading: Sentinel events: when harm demands a deep investigation
sections.body:
The Joint Commission uses the word sentinel (a guard who signals danger) because these events signal that something in the system is seriously wrong. The Joint Commission’s current definition: a sentinel event is a patient safety event, not primarily related to the natural course of the client’s illness or underlying condition, that reaches the client and results in death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm. (Older wording, still found in some textbooks and in the course source, described “an unexpected occurrence involving death or serious physical or psychological injury, or the risk thereof.”) The key ideas are unexpected and reached the client: a death from the expected course of a terminal illness is not a sentinel event; a death from a wrong-dose insulin infusion is. A near miss that was caught before reaching the client is reported but is not a sentinel event.

Three questions to classify any event. (1) Did it reach the client? If not, it is a near miss. (2) Was the harm caused by care rather than by the natural course of the illness? (3) Was the result death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm, or is the event on the Joint Commission’s always-qualifying list (wrong site, retained object, incompatible blood, suicide within 72 hours of discharge, and so on)? A “yes” to the first two plus either part of the third means sentinel event.

A sentinel event requires immediate investigation and a credible root cause analysis with an action plan. As a staff nurse, your role is to protect and assess the client, notify the provider and supervisor, preserve evidence (equipment, tubing, packaging, the medication), document facts in the record, and complete the incident report. The organization’s risk manager and leadership lead the analysis, and staff involved are interviewed to understand the system, not to assign blame.

rows: Unanticipated death or major permanent loss of function unrelated to the original illness
Respiratory arrest after unmonitored PCA opioid; client dies
Wrong client, wrong site, or wrong procedure
Surgery on the left knee instead of the right
Unintended retention of a foreign object
Sponge found on x-ray after abdominal surgery
Radiation overdose or wrong body region
Fluoroscopy far beyond planned dose
Incompatible blood transfusion (hemolytic reaction)
Type A client receives type B blood after an identification failure
Abduction, rape, assault, or homicide in the facility
Infant taken from a postpartum unit
Suicide in a staffed around-the-clock setting or within 72 hours of discharge
Client dies by suicide 2 days after discharge from inpatient psychiatry
Severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia
Newborn develops kernicterus after missed jaundice follow-up
Elopement from a staffed around-the-clock setting leading to death or serious harm
Resident with dementia leaves at night and is fatally injured

check.q: A client on hospice dies peacefully from metastatic cancer. A second client dies after receiving a 10-fold heparin overdose. Which is a sentinel event?
check.a: The heparin overdose death, because it was unexpected and caused by care rather than by the natural course of illness.

sections.heading: Clinical Exemplar B: Mr. Reuben Meyers
sections.body:
Mr. Reuben Meyers, 84, has Alzheimer’s disease and lives in an extended care facility. At 1:30 a.m. he wandered out of the building. He was struck in a hit-and-run accident at 2:08 a.m., staff discovered him missing at 2:15 a.m., and he died 12 days later. This is a sentinel event: elopement from a staffed around-the-clock setting leading to death. It also raises a potential breach of safety and monitoring standards. The facility must perform an immediate RCA2 and upgrade security, staffing, and risk-management systems.

Notice how an RCA2 team would think. The question is not “Which aide was assigned to him?” but “Why could a resident known to wander leave without an alarm sounding? Why did 45 minutes pass before anyone noticed? Were checks scheduled and documented? Was night staffing adequate for the number of residents at elopement risk? Were door alarms tested? Was a wander-management system (such as a bracelet that triggers door locks) used?” The action plan would include specific owners, deadlines, pilot tests, and measures, such as weekly door-alarm testing logs and missed-check rates.
sections.example: Appropriate risk-management upgrades after this event include an elopement-risk assessment on admission and with any change, a wander-management system, alarmed and regularly tested exits, scheduled and documented checks for at-risk residents, missing-resident drills, and staffing matched to resident acuity at night. Inappropriate responses include physically restraining or sedating all residents who wander, which create new harm and violate client rights.

check.q: Why is “retrain the night aide” alone a weak action after this event?
check.a: It targets one person, not the system weaknesses (alarms, checks, staffing, wander technology) that allowed the elopement to go unnoticed; RCA2 favors strong system-level actions.

sections.heading: Breach of care and risk management
sections.body:
A breach of care (breach of duty) occurs when a nurse deviates from the standard of care. Malpractice data (CRICO) show nurses are most often involved in breaches around bedside care (medication administration, monitoring IVs, catheters, and wounds), falls, pressure injuries, and communication breakdowns. These are exactly the areas where structured processes (barcode scanning, fall bundles, turning schedules, SBAR and read-back) protect both clients and nurses.

Risk management is the set of clinical and administrative systems, processes, and reports used to detect, monitor, assess, mitigate, and prevent risks. It has two faces. Proactive risk management prevents adverse events: environmental safety rounds, a failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) before implementing new infusion pumps, staff education, and policies. Reactive risk management minimizes damage after an event: incident report review, disclosure to the client and family, RCA, and claims management.

Patient dissatisfaction is a major risk factor for liability. Clients who feel ignored or disrespected are more likely to sue, even when care was technically adequate. The nurse’s best risk-reduction tool is often therapeutic communication: listen, acknowledge the concern, explain what will happen, follow through, and involve the charge nurse or patient advocate when needed. Arguing that “we did nothing wrong” or avoiding the room increases risk.

rows: FMEA before introducing new equipment or processes
Incident report review and trending
Environmental and fall-risk rounds
Root cause analysis after a sentinel event
Education and competency checks
Disclosure and apology to the client/family per policy
Policies such as two-identifier verification
Claims management and legal review

sections.heading: Incident reports and the response to an error
sections.body:
An incident (occurrence) report is a confidential, internal QI document. It is used to identify patterns and system problems, not to punish. Standard practice: complete it as soon as the client is safe, record objective facts (what you saw, what you did, who was notified, the client’s response), avoid opinions and blame, and send it to risk management or the designated manager per policy. Do not place it in the medical record, copy it, or write “incident report completed” in the chart; in the chart, document the clinical facts of the event and the care given. Report near misses too; they reveal the same weaknesses as actual errors.

When you discover a medication error, the order of actions is a classic NCLEX item.
steps: Assess the client first (vital signs and the specific effects of the drug, e.g., heart rate and BP after a beta blocker, glucose after insulin).
Intervene for immediate safety if needed (e.g., hold the next dose, call a rapid response if unstable).
Notify the provider and follow new orders; notify the charge nurse or manager.
Document the facts of what was given and the client’s condition and care in the medical record (without mentioning the incident report).
Complete the incident report per policy and participate in the review.
Disclose to the client per organizational policy, typically with the provider.

check.q: A nurse realizes she gave a client another client’s 50 mg metoprolol. What does she do first?
check.a: Assess the client (heart rate, blood pressure, symptoms of bradycardia or hypotension), because client safety comes before notifying, documenting, or reporting.

sections.heading: Root cause analysis (RCA2): fix the system
sections.body:
RCA2 (Improving Root Cause Analysis and Actions to Prevent Harm) is the modern standard for investigating serious events. It focuses on systems and processes, not individual performance. The team builds a timeline, asks “why?” repeatedly until it reaches causes the organization can control, and separates two kinds of variation. Special-cause variation is variation beyond normal, linked to something specific (a new protocol, a broken alarm, a staffing crisis on one night). Common-cause variation is the normal noise of the system; reducing it requires redesigning the system itself.

A credible RCA2 ends with an action plan: specific actions, responsible parties, timelines, pilot testing, and effectiveness metrics. Strong actions change the system (forcing functions, standardization, automation, staffing changes); weak actions rely on memory (reminders, “be more careful,” more training alone). FMEA is the proactive cousin of RCA: it asks “How could this fail?” before harm, whereas RCA asks “Why did this fail?” after.
sections.analogy: If water keeps appearing on the floor, mopping faster is a weak fix. RCA finds the leaking pipe. Special-cause variation is the night a pipe burst; common-cause variation is the slow drip the plumbing always had.
sections.example: Falls on a unit average 2–3 per month for a year. In March there are 9, all at night, after a new sedative-hypnotic order set was introduced. This is special-cause variation; the RCA focuses on the order set and night practices. If falls had stayed at 2–3 a month but the benchmark were 1, the problem would be common-cause variation, needing a redesign of the whole fall-prevention system.
steps: Secure the client and the scene: care for the client, preserve equipment and packaging, and report the event so the analysis can begin promptly.
Assemble an interprofessional team that includes frontline staff who know the process but were not directly involved, plus leaders who can approve changes.
Build a detailed timeline of what happened, using records, equipment data, and interviews conducted to understand the process, not to assign blame.

Ask “why?” at each step until you reach causes the organization controls (equipment design, storage, staffing, communication, policies), and decide whether the variation is special-cause or common-cause.
Choose actions, favoring strong system changes (forcing functions, standardization, automation, staffing) over weak ones (reminders, memos, “be more careful,” training alone).
Assign each action an owner and a deadline, pilot-test it, and define a measure (for example, weekly alarm-test logs or pump-library compliance).
Monitor the measures and share results with staff; if the measure does not improve, the action was not strong enough and the cycle continues.

sections.heading: Medication safety: errors, ADEs, and high-risk drugs
sections.body:
NCC MERP defines a medication error as any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or client harm while the medication is in the control of the health care professional, client, or consumer. An adverse drug event (ADE) is harm from exposure to a medication. The overlap is partial: a preventable ADE is an error that caused harm (wrong dose causes hypoglycemia); a non-preventable ADE is harm without error (first-time anaphylaxis to a correctly prescribed and given antibiotic in a client with no known allergy); and a medication error may cause no harm at all (a late dose with no effect).

High-risk medications include IV unfractionated heparin, ISMP look-alike, sound-alike (LASA) drugs (e.g., hydroxyzine/hydralazine), and Beers Criteria drugs in adults 65 and older (e.g., benzodiazepines, which increase falls and confusion). The nurse questions a Beers drug order in an older adult and suggests safer alternatives, and uses independent double checks for high-alert infusions per policy.

rows: Barcode scanning (client ID band + medication)
Wrong client, wrong drug, wrong dose
Scan every time; never scan a copied label or a band not on the client; report scanner failures instead of working around them
Tall-man lettering and regulating similar names
LASA confusion (hydrOXYzine vs. hydrALAZINE)
Read the full name; store LASA drugs apart; verify the indication
Pharmacy first-dose review
Wrong drug, dose, interaction, allergy
Wait for verification except in true emergencies per policy
Computerized Provider Order Entry (CPOE)
Illegible orders, transcription errors, missed interactions
Clarify unclear orders; limit verbal orders to emergencies and read back

check.q: A client with no known allergies develops hives after a correctly ordered and administered first dose of amoxicillin. Error, ADE, or both?
check.a: An ADE that is not a medication error, because harm occurred but no preventable deviation occurred. It must still be reported, treated, and documented, and the allergy recorded.

sections.heading: Staffing, nursing-sensitive indicators, resource use, and personal responsibility
sections.body:
Evidence consistently links higher RN skill mix (the proportion of nursing hours provided by RNs) and more nursing hours with fewer adverse outcomes: pressure injuries, gastritis and upper GI bleeding, acute MI, restraint use, failure to rescue, pneumonia, sepsis, UTI, shock/cardiac arrest, and 30-day mortality. The mechanism is surveillance: RNs recognize early deterioration and intervene. Replacing RNs with UAP may increase total hours but lowers skill mix, so it does not achieve the same effect. Box 50.2 (topic 2) organizes these nursing-sensitive indicators into structure, process, and outcome.

Resource utilization aims to cut waste: unnecessary procedures, excessive administrative costs, missed prevention, medical fraud, prolonged stays caused by medication errors, extra visits caused by poor client education, and time lost to poor equipment or documentation. Many forms of waste are also safety problems.

Healthy work environment and personal responsibility. The AACN’s six standards (skilled communication, true collaboration, effective decision-making, appropriate staffing, meaningful recognition, authentic leadership) create conditions where nurses speak up and errors are caught. Individually, students and nurses must never perform an act they are uncertain how to perform, must follow facility policies and procedures, and must report errors properly. Saying “I have not been checked off on that; I need supervision” is a safety behavior, not a weakness.
sections.example: A student nurse is asked by a busy staff RN to remove a chest tube “because it’s easy.” The student has never been taught or supervised in this skill and it may be outside the student role. The correct response is to decline to perform it independently, tell the RN that they have not been trained, and notify the clinical instructor; the student may observe if appropriate.

sections.heading: Blame-free environment vs. Just Culture
sections.body: A blame-free environment lets staff report errors and near misses without fear of punishment, so system problems surface. Its weakness, if taken alone, is that it can seem to excuse dangerous choices. Just Culture keeps the safety of reporting but adds accountability and zero tolerance for reckless behavior. It judges the behavior, not the outcome: a nurse who takes a reckless shortcut is accountable even if no harm occurred, and a nurse who makes an honest slip is consoled even if harm did occur.

rows: Human error
Inadvertent slip, lapse, or mistake while trying to do the right thing (e.g., transposing digits on a pump while interrupted; picking up a look-alike vial stored in the adjacent bin)
Console the person; fix the system (storage, interruptions, pump libraries)
At-risk behavior

A choice that drifts from rules, with risk not recognized or believed justified (e.g., skipping barcode scanning because the scanner is slow; pre-pouring medications; skipping two identifiers because “I know her”)
Coach: help the person see the risk; remove incentives for the shortcut; fix the barrier
Reckless behavior
Conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk (e.g., working under the influence of alcohol or narcotics; knowingly falsifying care)
Disciplinary (remedial or punitive) action; remove from care immediately when there is risk to clients

sections.analogy: Driving: a driver who misreads a confusing sign makes an error (fix the sign). A driver who rolls through stop signs because everyone does is at risk (coaching, maybe a ticket). A driver who drives drunk is reckless (license action).

check.q: A nurse bypasses the barcode scanner for three clients because it is slow and says everyone does it. No harm occurs. What category and response?
check.a: At-risk behavior (a shortcut with an unappreciated risk). The manager coaches the nurse and fixes the slow scanner so the safe behavior becomes the easy behavior. The lack of harm does not change the category.

steps: Separate the behavior from the outcome. Write down what the nurse did, and set aside whether harm occurred; Just Culture judges the choice, not the luck.

Ask: Did the nurse intend the action? If the nurse meant to do the right thing and slipped, lapsed, or made a mistake (transposed digits, grabbed the adjacent look-alike vial, forgot a step after an interruption), it is human error.

If the action was a choice, ask: Did the nurse recognize the risk? If the nurse took a shortcut believing it was safe or justified (“everyone does it,” “the scanner is too slow,” “I know this client”), it is at-risk behavior.

If the nurse knew the risk was substantial and unjustifiable and chose it anyway (working impaired, knowingly falsifying care, ignoring a known critical safety rule with no justification), it is reckless behavior.

Apply the substitution test: would another competent nurse in the same situation, with the same system pressures, likely have done the same thing? If yes, the system is driving the behavior and must be fixed along with any coaching.

Match the response: human error → console and fix the system; at-risk behavior → coach and remove the incentive or barrier; reckless behavior → remove from client care if clients are at risk, then disciplinary action and, for conduct issues, reporting per policy and law.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
The NC Board of Nursing (NCBON) regulates nursing under the Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.). The NCBON uses a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool for practice events that classifies human error vs. at-risk behavior vs. reckless behavior, mirroring the employer framework in this lesson. Many practice errors can be handled through employer remediation when the tool supports it.

Conduct issues are different. Drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches are reported to the Board rather than handled only by the employer. The NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for nurses with substance use disorders, which supports reporting an impaired colleague as a protective act for clients and the colleague. NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state, so a multistate license holder practicing in NC is accountable to NC law and the NCBON for practice here.

Elopement and abuse events involving disabled adults may also trigger mandatory reporting to the county DSS director under G.S. 108A-102 when a disabled adult needs protective services.

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes
sections.body: These pairs appear again and again in safety items.

headers: The clue that tells them apart
rows: Medication error vs. ADE
Error = preventable deviation (harm or not). ADE = harm from a drug (preventable or not).
Was there a deviation? Was there harm? Correctly given drug + harm = ADE without error.
Human error vs. At-risk behavior
Error = unintended slip. At-risk = chosen shortcut with unrecognized risk.
“Accidentally,” “while interrupted” → human error. “To save time,” “everyone does it” → at-risk.
At-risk vs. Reckless
At-risk = risk not recognized/believed justified. Reckless = conscious disregard of substantial risk.
Impairment, knowingly ignoring a known serious risk → reckless.
Blame-free vs. Just Culture
Blame-free = report without fear. Just Culture = report without fear plus accountability and zero tolerance for recklessness.
Any mention of consequences for reckless acts → Just Culture.
RCA vs. FMEA
RCA = after an event, why did it happen. FMEA = before, how could it fail.
“After the event” → RCA. “Before implementing” → FMEA (proactive risk management).
Special- vs. Common-cause variation
Special = unusual spike with a specific cause. Common = normal system noise.
Sudden change after a new factor → special. Stable but poor performance → common.
Sentinel event vs. Near miss
Sentinel = reached client with death or serious harm. Near miss = caught before reaching client.
Did it reach the client and cause serious harm?
Incident report vs. Chart documentation
Incident report = internal QI document, not in chart. Chart = clinical facts and care.
Never write “incident report filed” in the chart.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: errors, reporting, and Just Culture
sections.body:
Expect: (1) first-action items after an error (assess the client first); (2) incident-report SATA items (facts, timely, not in chart, no blame); (3) Just Culture classification with a charge nurse or manager response; (4) impaired colleague items (remove from care, notify supervisor); (5) “Which event is a sentinel event?” and RCA focus questions; (6) medication-safety items about barcode scanning workarounds, LASA drugs, and Beers Criteria; (7) student-role items (never perform an unfamiliar skill).

Sample question: The charge nurse notices that a staff nurse’s speech is slurred and smells alcohol on her breath at 0900. The nurse is assigned five clients. Which action should the charge nurse take first? (A) Document the observations and report them at the end of the shift. (B) Ask the nurse whether she has been drinking. (C) Relieve the nurse from client care and notify the nursing supervisor. (D) Reassign the nurse’s two most unstable clients to another nurse.
steps: Read the stem: objective cues (slurred speech, odor of alcohol) during active client care.
Identify what is asked: the first action; client safety is the priority.
Recognize the behavior category: working impaired is reckless behavior with substantial risk to clients.
Eliminate A: waiting until the end of the shift leaves five clients at risk for hours.
Eliminate B: confronting the nurse may be part of the process later, but it does not protect clients now and may escalate the situation.
Eliminate D: partial reassignment still leaves three clients with an impaired nurse.
Choose C: remove the risk to all clients immediately and follow the chain of command; the supervisor then follows policy (testing, reporting to the Board, referral).

check.q: Reusable strategy for colleague-behavior items?
check.a: Classify the behavior (error, at-risk, reckless), then ask what protects clients right now. If clients are at risk, remove the risk first and escalate through the chain of command; consoling or coaching comes afterward.

sections.heading: Worked case: the heparin near miss and the wrong-dose event
sections.body: You are working nights on a medical unit. At 2200 a float nurse nearly hangs a heparin bag labeled 25,000 units/250 mL instead of the 25,000 units/500 mL bag ordered; you catch it during the independent double check. At 0300 the same week, another nurse programs a heparin infusion (25,000 units/500 mL) at 200 mL/hr instead of the ordered 20 mL/hr while being interrupted by an alarm, a 10-fold overdose; the client’s aPTT at 0600 is critically high and the client has gum bleeding.
steps: Recognize cues: two heparin events in one week involving a high-alert drug; one near miss, one error with harm (a preventable ADE).

Take action for the client with bleeding first: stop the infusion, assess vital signs, bleeding, and neurologic status, notify the provider immediately, and follow orders (e.g., protamine if ordered, repeat labs).
Document the clinical facts in the record; complete incident reports for both the near miss and the error; do not chart that a report was filed.
Classify behavior: the programming slip while interrupted is human error (console the nurse); the bag selection near miss suggests a storage or labeling system problem.

Analyze with RCA principles: two concentrations stored together (LASA risk), interruptions during programming, pump drug library not used. Ask whether these are special-cause (new supplier bag) or common-cause (always stored together).

Generate strong system actions: one standard heparin concentration, pump drug library with hard limits, no-interruption zone during high-alert programming, independent double check, owners and deadlines assigned.
Evaluate: track heparin-related near misses and errors and pump library compliance monthly as effectiveness metrics.

check.q: Why should the 2200 near miss be reported even though no harm occurred?
check.a: Near misses reveal the same system weakness (look-alike concentrations stored together) that can later cause harm; reporting lets the organization fix it before a client is injured.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 50 study guide, pp. 2856–2859 (50.4 steps 3–4: sentinel events and Joint Commission list, breach of care and CRICO data, risk management and patient dissatisfaction, Clinical Exemplar B, RCA2, medication errors and ADEs, high-risk medications, safety interventions, staffing and NDNQI Box 50.2, resource utilization, blame-free environment vs. Just Culture, AACN standards, personal responsibility).

Clarifications: (1) The Joint Commission revised its sentinel event definition; it now describes a patient safety event not primarily related to the natural course of illness that results in death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm. The older phrase “or the risk thereof” in the source reflects the earlier definition. (2) The source groups “abduction, rape, assault, homicide, or suicide in facility or within 72 hours of discharge.” In Joint Commission policy the 72-hour post-discharge window applies to suicide; abduction, rape, assault, and homicide refer to events while the client is receiving care on site. (3) RCA2 stands for “Root Cause Analysis and Action” and was published by the National Patient Safety Foundation (now part of IHI). (4) Incident-report practices, the medication-error response sequence, FMEA, near misses, and strong vs. weak actions are standard nursing and patient-safety content added because they apply this topic.

mnemonics.name: Console, Coach, Consequence (Just Culture)
mnemonics.text: Human error → Console (and fix the system). At-risk behavior → Coach. Reckless behavior → Consequence (discipline). Judge the behavior, not the outcome.

mnemonics.name: A-N-D-I after a medication error
mnemonics.text: Assess the client, Notify the provider (and charge nurse), Document facts in the chart, Incident report (not in the chart).

pearls: After any error, assess the client first; paperwork never comes before physiology.
Incident reports are factual, timely, blame-free, and never mentioned in or filed with the chart.
Report near misses; they are free lessons about system weakness.
RCA2 asks why the system allowed the event, not who to blame, and ends with owners, timelines, and metrics.
An ADE can occur without an error; an error can occur without an ADE.
Higher RN skill mix reduces failure to rescue; more UAP hours do not substitute for RN surveillance.
Workarounds such as skipping the scanner are at-risk behavior: coach the person and fix the barrier.
Never perform a skill you are unsure of; ask for supervision and follow policy.
redFlags: A colleague with slurred speech, alcohol odor, or unexplained narcotic discrepancies must be removed from client care and reported up the chain of command now.
Any unexpected death or serious harm from care (wrong site, retained object, wrong blood, elopement with harm) is a sentinel event requiring immediate reporting.
Repeated barcode overrides or pre-poured medications on a unit signal normalized at-risk behavior.
A Beers Criteria drug (e.g., a benzodiazepine) ordered for an older adult at fall risk should be questioned.
A sudden spike in an indicator after a new process is special-cause variation that needs prompt investigation.
recap: Sentinel events are unexpected events causing death or serious harm and require immediate investigation and RCA.
Breach of care is deviation from the standard; nurses’ breaches cluster in bedside care, falls, pressure injuries, and communication.
Risk management has proactive (prevent, FMEA) and reactive (minimize damage, RCA, disclosure) parts; dissatisfaction raises liability risk.
RCA2 focuses on systems, separates special- and common-cause variation, and produces actionable, measured plans.
Medication errors are preventable events; ADEs are harm; high-risk drugs include IV heparin, LASA drugs, and Beers drugs in older adults.
Barcode scanning, tall-man lettering, pharmacy first-dose review, and CPOE are system safeguards.
RN skill mix and nursing hours reduce adverse outcomes, including failure to rescue.
Just Culture: console human error, coach at-risk behavior, discipline reckless behavior.

checks.q: A nurse accidentally hangs the wrong IV antibiotic because two bags with similar labels were stored in the same bin. What is the Just Culture category and the best organizational response?
checks.a: Human error. Console the nurse and fix the system (separate storage, distinct labels, barcode scanning).

checks.q: A client is angry that his call light went unanswered for 30 minutes and says he will sue. What is the best risk-reduction response?
checks.a: Listen, acknowledge his concern, address his immediate needs, explain follow-up, and involve the charge nurse or patient advocate. Dissatisfaction drives liability; defensiveness increases it.

checks.q: Which is stronger after a fall: “remind staff to use bed alarms” or “bed alarms auto-activate when the bed is placed in low position for high-risk clients”? Why?
checks.a: Auto-activation is stronger because it is a forcing function that does not depend on memory; reminders are weak actions.

checks.q: Your unit’s falls jump from 2 to 8 in one month after a new sleep medication order set. What type of variation is this and what should the RCA focus on?
checks.a: Special-cause variation; the RCA should examine the new order set and associated practices.

checks.q: A student is asked to insert an NG tube without supervision and has only practiced in the lab. What should the student do?
checks.a: Decline to perform it independently, explain they have not been checked off, and contact the instructor or RN for supervision per policy.

checks.q: An 80-year-old client at high fall risk has a new order for lorazepam at bedtime for sleep. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Question the order with the provider because benzodiazepines are Beers Criteria drugs that increase fall and confusion risk in older adults; suggest nonpharmacologic sleep measures or safer alternatives.
